credit.author: See the Commons file page

items.summary: A heavy, angled clamp with broad triangular serrated jaws designed to control haemorrhage from the caesarean uterine incision.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Heavy, sturdy stainless steel instrument with finger ring handles, ratchet lock, and angled or straight shanks.
Blades terminate in broad, flattened, triangular or trapezoidal plates lined with deep transverse serrations.
The broad clamping surface compresses a large swath of tissue simultaneously.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Applied to the cut edges and lateral angles of the uterine incision during lower segment caesarean section (LSCS).
Compreses the full thickness of the bleeding myometrial margins to control venous and arterial haemorrhage before closing.
Aids in elevating and exposing the uterine flap edges for accurate anatomical approximation during suturing.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Specifically engineered for haemostasis of the pregnant myometrium during caesarean birth.
The broad blades distribute pressure across several centimetres, avoiding the focal tearing caused by narrow artery forceps.

viva.q: What is the primary clinical application of Green-Armytage forceps in obstetrics?
viva.a: It is applied along the cut margins and lateral angles of the lower segment caesarean uterine incision to secure immediate haemostasis.

viva.q: Why are Green-Armytage clamps superior to standard artery forceps on the uterine incision?
viva.a: Their broad, flat triangular jaws compress a wide area of vascular myometrium without cutting through the oedematous tissue.

image.brief: Sturdy Green-Armytage forceps on a neutral background showing heavy ring handles, ratchet lock, and broad flat triangular serrated tips.

items.summary: An atraumatic ratcheted forceps with broad triangular fenestrated loops and smooth transverse ridges for handling tubular organs.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Long-handled instrument with finger rings, ratchet lock, and outward-bowed shanks.
Jaws expand into smooth, triangular or oval fenestrated loops with rounded edges and no sharp teeth.
The grasping rims meet smoothly to cradle viscera without increasing intraluminal pressure.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Holding and stabilising the fallopian tubes during tubal ligation (Pomeroy or Parkland tubectomy) and salpingectomy.
Grasping delicate loops of bowel during exploratory laparotomy and bowel resection-anastomosis.
Holding the appendix during appendicectomy and supporting the ureter during retroperitoneal pelvic dissection.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Completely non-perforating and atraumatic design; grips tubular structures without puncturing the serosa or occluding lumens.
Standard instrument for picking up the fallopian tube at its ampullary-isthmic loop during surgical sterilisation.

viva.q: Why is Babcock forceps chosen to hold the fallopian tube during female sterilisation?
viva.a: Its broad, smooth fenestrated loop cradles the tube securely without crushing the muscular wall or compromising tubal vessels.

viva.q: What mechanical feature ensures that Babcock forceps remains atraumatic?
viva.a: The lack of sharp teeth and the presence of rounded, fenestrated jaws that distribute holding tension over a wide surface area.

image.brief: Babcock tissue forceps lying open on a surgical drape with distinct smooth triangular fenestrated jaws visible in profile.

credit.generated: Illustration created with MaiK (StewardMD AI) and checked against the real instrument shape

items.summary: A slender metallic probe terminating in a small backward-facing hook, used to retrieve an intrauterine device with missing strings.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Slender, solid stainless steel probe featuring a flat handle at one end and a small angled hook at the other.
Resembles a uterine sound in overall gauge and length, but has no calibration markings.
The hook end possesses a subtle distal angulation to assist engagement within the endometrial cavity.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Retrieving an intrauterine contraceptive device (IUCD, Copper T) when the retrieval threads are missing at the external os.
Used following ultrasound confirmation that the contraceptive device remains situated inside the uterine cavity.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Must only be employed after imaging excludes extrauterine pelvic translocation of the device.
Blind manipulation carries risks of cervical laceration, endometrial trauma, and uterine perforation.
If gentle rotation fails to hook the device, hysteroscopic retrieval under direct visual guidance is indicated.

viva.q: What investigation must precede the use of an IUD hook for missing strings?
viva.a: Pelvic ultrasonography or abdominal radiography to confirm that the intrauterine device is truly present within the endometrial cavity.

viva.q: What are the primary hazards associated with repeated passes of an IUD hook?
viva.a: Trauma to the endocervical canal, creation of a false passage, endometrial denudation, and uterine wall perforation.

image.brief: Fine stainless steel IUD hook resting flat on white paper highlighting the slender shaft, flat handle, and miniature terminal hook.

items.summary: A corkscrew-shaped traction instrument with a transverse handle used to obtain a solid mechanical purchase on uterine fibroids.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Heavy stainless steel instrument with a transverse T-shaped or oval loop handle at one end.
Terminal end consists of a sharp, tapered metallic helical corkscrew.
Engineered to bore securely into dense, rubbery fibroid parenchyma.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Providing traction, elevation, and leverage on uterine leiomyomas during abdominal myomectomy.
Assisting enucleation and traction of fibroids during vaginal myomectomy.
Inserted into an enlarged myomatous uterus to manipulate and stabilise the organ during difficult pelvic surgery.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Must be screwed strictly into the pseudo-capsule and centre of the fibroid, never into normal myometrium or vascular margins.
Rotated clockwise to engage and counter-clockwise to disengage after enucleation.
If placed too deeply or near the base, it can cause severe haemorrhage from large dilated capsular veins.

viva.q: What is the primary surgical purpose of a myoma screw?
viva.a: It screws into the substance of a uterine fibroid to provide traction and leverage, facilitating surgical enucleation from its pseudocapsule.

viva.q: Where should the myoma screw be anchored within the tumour?
viva.a: Directly into the solid fibrous core of the leiomyoma, avoiding vascular peripheral capsules and normal myometrial tissue.

image.brief: Metallic Doyen myoma screw shown with oval handle and sharp spiralling helical corkscrew tip on plain medical backdrop.

items.summary: A specialised curved vascular clamp designed to temporarily compress the bilateral uterine arteries at the internal os during myomectomy.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Heavy, broad stainless steel clamp with angled ring handles, a locking ratchet, and curved, atraumatic padded or serrated blades.
Blades are curved to encircle the lower uterine isthmus and compress both uterine vessels laterally.
Engineered to occlude the uterine arterial supply while protecting the cervix and bladder base.

blocks.title: Surgical technique and use
bullets: Applied across the lower uterine segment at the level of the internal os after reflecting the bladder peritoneum.
Temporarily compresses bilateral uterine vessels to achieve an almost bloodless field while incising and enucleating fibroids.
Combined with atraumatic rubber-shod clamps on both infundibulopelvic ligaments to occlude collateral ovarian vessels.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Uterine clamp time should be monitored, releasing the clamp periodically to avoid prolonged ischaemic injury to the uterus.
The bladder must be dissected downwards prior to clamp placement to prevent accidental bladder crushing.

viva.q: Where is the Bonney myomectomy clamp applied during surgery?
viva.a: Across the lower uterine segment at the level of the internal os, after mobilising and reflecting the bladder peritoneum downward.

viva.q: What additional vascular clamp is placed alongside the Bonney clamp during myomectomy?
viva.a: Atraumatic clamps on the infundibulopelvic ligaments to occlude the ovarian arterial collateral circulation to the uterus.

image.brief: Bonney myomectomy clamp with curved broad blades, angled shanks, and ratchet lock displayed horizontally on surgical towel.

items.summary: A heavy ratcheted surgical clamp with short jaws and cross-hatched serrations engineered to grip curved suture needles firmly.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Heavy instrument featuring long shanks with finger rings, a firm multi-step ratchet lock, and short, sturdy jaws.
Inner faces of the jaws possess cross-hatched (criss-cross) serrations and a central longitudinal groove to seat curved needles.
Significantly shorter blade-to-handle ratio compared to an artery forceps to maximise mechanical holding leverage.

blocks.title: Comparison with artery forceps
bullets: Needle holder is heavier and more rigid with short jaws, criss-cross serrations, and a needle groove.
Artery forceps is lighter with longer blades, transverse parallel serrations, and no central needle-retaining groove.

blocks.title: Rules for holding needles
bullets: The needle should be grasped at the junction of the anterior two-thirds and posterior one-third of its shaft.
Holding too near the tip reduces mechanical drive; holding at the swaged eye risks bending or snapping the needle.
The needle tip must point perpendicular to the jaws to maintain control during tissue penetration.

viva.q: Where along a curved suture needle should the needle holder grasp?
viva.a: At the junction of the anterior two-thirds and posterior one-third of the needle shaft, avoiding both the delicate tip and the eye.

viva.q: How do you distinguish a needle holder from an artery forceps on physical inspection?
viva.a: A needle holder has noticeably shorter, sturdier jaws with cross-hatched serrations and a central groove, whereas an artery forceps has longer transversely-serrated jaws.

image.brief: Mayo-Hegar needle holder on white surface with jaws open showing cross-hatched tungsten carbide inserts and central longitudinal groove.

items.summary: Spring-action handheld thumb forceps available with terminal interlocking teeth or smooth serrations for tissue handling.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Pair of metallic spring blades joined at the base, held between thumb and fingers without finger rings or ratchets.
Toothed forceps (e.g. Lane or Treves) terminates in a 1x2 interlocking sharp tooth-and-socket mechanism.
Non-toothed dissecting forceps terminates in blunt, rounded tips with transverse ridges and grooves.

groups.label: Toothed dissecting forceps
bullets: Grasping tough structural tissues including skin, scalp, and rectus sheath during incisional entry, dissection, and suturing.
Provides an exceptionally secure, slip-free grip that avoids crushing large tissue areas.

groups.label: Non-toothed dissecting forceps
bullets: Grasping delicate, friable viscera including peritoneum, myometrium, bladder margins, and bowel.
Manipulating surgical gauze and swabs during dressing and pack application.
Safely loading and unloading surgical scalpel blades onto BP handles.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Toothed forceps must never be applied to bowel, bladder, or blood vessels because teeth puncture and tear fragile walls.
Non-toothed forceps holds by friction compression; excessive squeeze pressure can crush delicate tissue edges.

viva.q: When is a toothed dissecting forceps selected over a non-toothed forceps?
viva.a: When manipulating tough, resilient tissues like skin and rectus sheath, where terminal teeth prevent slippage without crushing.

viva.q: Why is toothed forceps strictly contraindicated on hollow pelvic organs?
viva.a: The sharp teeth readily pierce and lacerate thin muscular walls of the bowel, bladder, or blood vessels, causing perforation.

image.brief: Side-by-side display of toothed dissecting forceps showing 1x2 teeth and non-toothed forceps showing transverse grooved jaws on white linen.

items.summary: A reusable metallic Bard-Parker scalpel handle fitted with interchangeable disposable surgical steel blades for incising tissue.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Reusable flat stainless steel handle with a slotted bayonet fitting at the tip to mount disposable blades.
Handle number 4 is large and broad, designed to fit large heavy blades (such as blade numbers 20, 21, 22, 23).
Handle number 3 is slender and compact, designed to mount smaller precision blades (such as blade numbers 10, 11, 15).

blocks.title: Uses and blade combinations
bullets: Handle number 4 with curved belly blade number 22 is standard for primary abdominal laparotomy and thoracotomy incisions.
Handle number 3 with small curved blade number 15 is used for fine dissection, plastic trimming, and precise angles.
Handle number 3 with sharp-pointed blade number 11 is used for stab incisions to drain abscesses and place trocars.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Named after Morgan Parker and C.R. Bard who introduced the detachable blade system.
Blades must always be mounted and dismounted using a needle holder or non-toothed forceps, never with bare fingers.

viva.q: Which Bard-Parker handle and blade combination is standard for opening the abdomen in caesarean section?
viva.a: Handle number 4 fitted with blade number 20 or 22, providing a broad curved cutting belly for long skin incisions.

viva.q: How should a disposable scalpel blade be loaded and unloaded safely?
viva.a: Using a needle holder or heavy artery forceps to grip the blade base and slide it onto the track, keeping fingers away from the sharp edge.

image.brief: Stainless steel BP handle number 4 shown with detachable number 22 surgical blade mounted, alongside a number 3 handle on white background.

items.summary: Heavy, thick-bladed surgical scissors available in straight and curved forms designed for cutting dense tissues and fascial planes.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Stout, robust scissors with thick blades and beveled cutting edges terminating in semi-blunt rounded tips.
Blade-to-handle length ratio is approximately 1 to 2, providing formidable mechanical cutting leverage.
Available as straight Mayo scissors or curved Mayo scissors in lengths from 14 cm to 23 cm.

groups.label: Straight Mayo scissors
bullets: Cutting tough tissues near the surface of a wound.
Cutting heavy surgical sutures, drains, and gauze dressings.

groups.label: Curved Mayo scissors
bullets: Cutting and dissecting dense fibrous structures including rectus sheath, aponeurosis, uterine ligaments, and heavy muscle.
Provides deeper reach into the pelvic cavity while maintaining visualisation beyond the curve.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Engineered for tough tissues; delicate visceral layers must not be dissected with Mayo scissors to avoid blunt tearing.
Using curved Mayo scissors to cut wire or bone dulls the cutting bevel.

viva.q: What is the primary surgical role of curved Mayo scissors in gynaecological laparotomy?
viva.a: Cutting dense, thick fibrous tissues such as the rectus sheath fascia and heavy uterine ligaments during hysterectomy.

viva.q: How do straight and curved Mayo scissors differ in clinical utility?
viva.a: Straight Mayo scissors are used for superficial tissue cutting and trimming heavy sutures, while curved scissors divide deep thick tissues.

image.brief: Pair of heavy curved stainless steel Mayo dissecting scissors beside a straight pair on a plain blue surgical field.

items.summary: Slender, long-handled surgical scissors with delicate, blunt-tipped blades designed specifically for fine soft tissue dissection.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Elegant surgical scissors with long, slender shanks and relatively short, delicate cutting blades.
High handle-to-blade ratio provides precision tactile feedback during delicate tissue dissection.
Blades terminate in rounded, semi-blunt tips, available in curved and straight designs.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Dissecting fine, delicate tissue planes including uterovesical peritoneal fold and pelvic retroperitoneal spaces.
Mobilising the bladder flap off the lower uterine segment in caesarean section and hysterectomy.
Widely utilised across gynaecological, general, dermatological, and plastic surgical operations.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Strict rule: never use Metzenbaum scissors to cut sutures, surgical drains, or thick fibrous fascia.
Cutting suture materials rapidly dulls and misaligns the fine precision cutting edges.

viva.q: Why is it strictly forbidden to cut sutures with Metzenbaum scissors?
viva.a: Suture filaments notch and dull the delicate, finely honed cutting blades, ruining them for fine anatomical dissection.

viva.q: What anatomical dissection step in caesarean section typically utilises Metzenbaum scissors?
viva.a: Incising the loose uterovesical peritoneum and gently pushing down the bladder flap to expose the lower uterine segment.

image.brief: Curved Metzenbaum scissors showing long slender handles and short, delicate rounded cutting blades on neutral background.

items.summary: Heavy angled surgical scissors with an obtuse bend and rounded lower probe blade designed for making perineal episiotomy incisions.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Non-ratcheted finger ring scissors featuring a distinct lateral angulation of approximately 45 degrees between shanks and blades.
The lower blade features a broad, flattened, semi-blunt tip designed to slide over the presenting foetal head without scratch injury.
The upper blade is sharp and sturdy to divide tough perineal skin and pelvic musculature in a single clean cut.

blocks.title: Clinical indications and incision types
bullets: Performed during crowning in the second stage of labour to facilitate delivery and prevent irregular third-degree anal sphincter tears.
Right mediolateral episiotomy (RMLE): initiated from the posterior fourchette and directed 60 to 80 degrees laterally towards the right.
Left mediolateral episiotomy (LMLE): directed downwards and laterally towards the left ischial tuberosity.
Median episiotomy: midline posterior cut towards the anus, offering easier repair but carrying higher risk of anal sphincter disruption.

blocks.title: Anatomical structures divided
bullets: Posterior vaginal wall mucosa and submucosa.
Perineal skin and subcutaneous fatty tissue.
Superficial and deep transverse perineal muscles and bulbospongiosus muscle fibres.

viva.q: Why are the blades of Braun episiotomy scissors angled relative to the handle?
viva.a: The angulation keeps the operator hand flat against the maternal perineum, directing the blades along the pelvic outlet axis.

viva.q: Which anatomical muscles are divided when performing a mediolateral episiotomy?
viva.a: The bulbospongiosus muscle and the superficial and deep transverse perineal muscles.

viva.q: What is the primary advantage of a mediolateral episiotomy over a midline episiotomy?
viva.a: It directs tearing away from the anal verge, substantially lowering the incidence of third-degree and fourth-degree perineal lacerations.

image.brief: Angled Braun episiotomy scissors shown on white surface highlighting the distinct bend in the shanks and blunt rounded lower blade.

items.summary: Specialised scissors featuring a hook-shaped notch on the lower blade designed to slip under tight surgical knots without pulling tissue.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Compact scissors with short blades and comfortable finger loops.
The lower blade features a small concave crescentic notch near its tip.
The notch lifts the suture thread away from the skin surface and prevents the loop from slipping out during transection.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Cutting and removing cutaneous and mucosal sutures post-operatively.
Safely dividing skin closure stitches following caesarean section, laparotomy, or perineal repair.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: The blunt hooked tip is slid gently under the suture knot with the flat surface resting against the patient skin.
Not intended for tissue dissection or dividing heavy wire sutures.

viva.q: What is the function of the notch on the blade of suture cutting scissors?
viva.a: It hooks under the suture loop beneath the knot, elevating the thread and holding it securely so it cuts without dragging skin.

viva.q: Why should suture scissors not be used for tissue dissection?
viva.a: The hooked blade is designed solely for picking up thin threads; attempting tissue dissection causes blunt tearing and crushes wound margins.

image.brief: Spencer stitch cutting scissors lying flat on sterile drape with close-up view of the small hooked notch on the lower cutting blade.

items.summary: A ratcheted surgical clamp with sharp inward-curving pointed jaws used to fix sterile surgical drapes to the patient skin.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Scissor-pattern steel instrument with finger rings, ratchet lock, and sharply curved, inward-pointing needle-sharp tips.
When closed, the sharp pointed tips meet or overlap to puncture and lock through fabric layers.
Non-perforating varieties feature broad, flat rubber-shod or ball-ended jaws for disposable non-woven paper drapes.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Securing sterile fabric drapes around the operative site to create an aseptic surgical field in anaesthetised patients.
Clamping and neatly anchoring electrosurgical diathermy cables, suction tubes, and camera cords to sterile drapes.
Occasionally used as an emergency skin retractor during minor procedures such as open appendicectomy when retractors are unavailable.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Sharp tips puncture the patient skin if clamped carelessly; verify drape depth before closing the ratchet.
Once clamped through skin or soiled drapes, removing and reapplying the same clip contaminates the sterile field.

viva.q: What is the primary function of Backhaus towel clips in the operating theatre?
viva.a: To secure sterile drapes around the operative site and anchor suction tubing and diathermy cables safely away from the incision.

viva.q: Why must towel clips not be unclamped and repositioned during a procedure?
viva.a: Because the tips have punctured drapes and potentially skin; moving them introduces microorganisms into the sterile field.

image.brief: Backhaus towel clip displayed with ring handles, ratchet lock, and sharp intersecting curved caliper tips on white surface.

items.summary: A disposable, hinged plastic clamp with locking serrated jaws used to permanently occlude the neonatal umbilical cord vessels.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Single-use medical-grade plastic clamp with a living hinge at one end and an irreversible locking clasp at the other.
Inner clamping surfaces feature grooved interlocking serrations designed to grip the gelatinous Wharton jelly without slippage.

blocks.title: Timing and physiological benefits
bullets: Applied after delivery following delayed cord clamping for 30 to 60 seconds with the neonate kept at or below placental level.
Delayed clamping transfers 50 to 80 mL of placental blood to the neonate, enriching iron stores and stem cell counts.
Benefits: reduces iron deficiency anaemia in infancy and decreases intraventricular haemorrhage in preterm neonates.
Active management of third stage of labour: uterotonic administration, controlled cord traction, and delayed cord clamping.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Applied 2 to 3 cm from the neonatal abdominal wall; an auxiliary clamp is placed further along before dividing the cord.
Immediate early cord clamping is reserved for situations requiring immediate neonatal resuscitation or maternal compromise.

viva.q: What is the recommended timing for clamping the umbilical cord in an uncompromised term infant?
viva.a: Delayed cord clamping for at least thirty to sixty seconds after birth, allowing placental transfusion of blood to the neonate.

viva.q: What are the primary clinical advantages of delayed cord clamping?
viva.a: Reduced infant iron deficiency anaemia, improved haemoglobin levels, and lowered rates of intraventricular haemorrhage in preterm infants.

items.summary: An angulated ligature-passing instrument designed to safely drive sutures through the sacrospinous ligament for vault suspension.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Long, slender vaginal instrument with a contoured handle and an angled shaft ending in a curved needle-carrying mechanism.
Specifically angulated to navigate through the pararectal space to reach the deep pelvic sidewall and ischial spine.
Curved tip holds and drives a ligature through the tough fibrous substance of the sacrospinous ligament.

blocks.title: Uses and advantages
bullets: Securing the prolapsed vaginal vault to the sacrospinous ligament in vaginal sacrospinous ligament fixation (sacrocolpopexy).
Provides clear exposure and accurate ligature application in deep, confined vaginal operative fields.
Minimises blood loss and limits extensive blunt dissection, keeping the pararectal space safer.
Reduces the risk of inadvertent trauma to the pudendal nerve, pudendal vessels, sciatic nerve, and inferior gluteal vessels.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Deschamps ligature carrier is an alternative instrument with an angled tip used for guiding sutures through deep pelvic structures.
Ligature must be placed 1.5 to 2 cm medial to the ischial spine to avoid injury to the internal pudendal neurovascular bundle.

viva.q: In which pelvic reconstructive operation is the Miya hook primarily employed?
viva.a: Vaginal sacrospinous ligament fixation, to suspend a prolapsed vaginal vault to the sacrospinous ligament.

viva.q: What major anatomical neurovascular structures are at risk during sacrospinous ligament suture placement?
viva.a: The pudendal nerve, internal pudendal vessels, sciatic nerve, and inferior gluteal vessels passing near the ischial spine.

image.brief: Miya hook ligature carrier showing slender handle, bayonet shaft, and curved suture-passing needle tip on surgical background.

items.summary: A large hand-held metallic abdominal retractor shaped like a question mark, used for deep pelvic and visceral retraction.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Curved, flat stainless steel strip shaped like a question mark or letter C with smooth rounded edges.
Features an ergonomic handle at one end and a broad, curved blade at the other without sharp edges.
Available in multiple widths ranging from narrow to broad deep blades.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Retracting the abdominal wall, bowel, and pelvic viscera during exploratory laparotomy and abdominal hysterectomy.
Holding back the urinary bladder and intestines to maintain an illuminated, clear deep operative field.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Hand-held and non-self-retaining, requiring constant manual positioning by a surgical assistant.
Atraumatic due to polished smooth contours, but prolonged forceful traction can cause visceral bruising.

viva.q: What is the defining shape and principal use of the Deaver retractor?
viva.a: Shaped like a question mark, it is used to hold back bowel and the abdominal wall for deep pelvic exposure during laparotomy.

viva.q: Why must an assistant be careful when holding a Deaver retractor against bowel?
viva.a: Excessive or unyielding localized pressure can cause serosal tearing or ischaemic bruising of retracted intestinal loops.

image.brief: Stainless steel Deaver retractor displaying characteristic question-mark curvature on white medical background.

items.summary: A handheld right-angled retractor with a flat blade designed to retract superficial abdominal layers and wound margins.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Handheld metal instrument featuring a flat handle and a single right-angled, flat downward-turned blade.
The distal blade end is slightly lipped to prevent slipping out from beneath the retracted tissue shelf.
Manufactured in diverse blade lengths and depths for superficial and mid-depth incisions.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Retracting skin, subcutaneous fat, and muscle margins during opening and closure of abdominal incisions.
Provides exposure and aids haemostasis by exerting direct compression on wound edges across pelvic procedures.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Ideal for small incisions or initial superficial layers of laparotomy before deep retractors are inserted.
Requires continuous manual holding by an assistant.

viva.q: What is the primary role of the Langenbeck retractor in abdominal surgery?
viva.a: Retracting superficial wound layers such as skin, fat, and fascia to improve access during laparotomy incision and closure.

viva.q: How does the Langenbeck retractor help with operative haemostasis?
viva.a: Its flat blade compresses subcutaneous microvessels along the incision margin while keeping the operative field clear.

image.brief: Langenbeck retractor with right-angled flat blade and teardrop-window handle displayed flat on sterile grey cloth.

items.summary: A sturdy handheld abdominal retractor with a broad, curved, rectangular blade used for retracting the abdominal wall and bladder.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Heavy stainless steel retractor with a long flat handle providing a firm mechanical purchase.
Blade is roughly square or rectangular with curved edges and a blunt, smooth lip.
Available as a single-ended instrument or double-ended with differing blade widths on either side.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Retracting the abdominal wall during abdominal hysterectomy, ovarian debulking, and caesarean section.
Retracting the abdominal wall in exploratory laparotomy for ruptured ectopic pregnancy and Wertheim hysterectomy.
Retracting the bladder during lower abdominal and pelvic surgical interventions.
Blunt smooth edge prevents trauma and reduces minor oozing from incision edges.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Hand-held and non-self-retaining, requiring assistant support.
Provides broad visceral retraction without the sharp corners that could injure neighbouring organs.

viva.q: What procedures in gynaecology frequently use the Morris retractor?
viva.a: Abdominal hysterectomy, caesarean section, exploratory laparotomy for ectopic pregnancy, and ovarian tumour debulking.

viva.q: Why is the blade of the Morris retractor curved with a blunt lip?
viva.a: To hold back the abdominal wall and urinary bladder securely without causing tissue laceration or puncturing blood vessels.

image.brief: Sturdy Morris retractor showing broad rectangular downward-curved blade and textured long handle on clean background.

items.summary: A handheld retractor featuring a wide, curved saddle-shaped blade and thumb-rest hook designed to protect the urinary bladder.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Sturdy metallic instrument featuring a broad, concave-convex saddle-shaped blade with rounded blunt edges.
Handle possesses a comfortable handgrip with a curved terminal hook or thumb rest for steady traction.
The wide curved blade is specifically contoured to cradle the dome of the bladder.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Widening lower abdominal incisions and retracting the bladder downward during lower segment caesarean section (LSCS).
Inserted before uterine incision to safeguard the bladder, removed prior to delivery of the foetal head, and reinserted for repair.
Retracting the anterior pelvic wall and bladder during abdominal hysterectomy and pelvic surgery.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Crucial timing rule: must be removed immediately before delivering the foetal head through the uterine incision to prevent cranial impaction.
Non-self-retaining retractor requiring manual maintenance by an assistant.

viva.q: At what critical moment during a caesarean section must the Doyen retractor be removed?
viva.a: Immediately prior to delivering the foetal head through the lower segment hysterotomy, preventing cranial obstruction or trauma.

viva.q: What anatomical structure does the Doyen retractor primarily protect during caesarean entry?
viva.a: The urinary bladder, which is retracted downward and shielded from accidental sharp incision while opening the lower uterine segment.

image.brief: Doyen retractor resting on a surgical table showing wide curved saddle blade and hollow handle with terminal recurved hook.

items.summary: A heavy self-retaining frame retractor with lateral spreading arms and an adjustable central bladder blade for extensive laparotomy.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Comprises a transverse frame with two lateral spreading arms fitted with solid or fenestrated wire blades.
Equipped with an adjustable central third arm supporting a curved, downward-reaching bladder blade.
Wing-nut or ratchet locking assembly maintains steady self-retaining mechanical separation of abdominal margins.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Providing hands-free lateral and inferior exposure of the abdominal cavity during major gynaecological laparotomy.
Used in radical hysterectomy, ovarian cytoreductive surgery, and combined pelvic and bowel resections.
Eliminates the requirement for multiple surgical assistants to manually hold retractors.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Moist laparotomy sponges should be placed between the lateral metal blades and the abdominal wall to protect muscle.
Excessive lateral spreading force risks compressing the femoral nerve against the psoas muscle, causing post-op femoral neuropathy.

viva.q: What is the key operative advantage of the Balfour self-retaining retractor?
viva.a: It maintains stable three-way abdominal retraction continuously without fatigue, freeing assistant hands for surgical tasks.

viva.q: What peripheral nerve can suffer compression injury from an improperly positioned Balfour retractor?
viva.a: The femoral nerve, which can be compressed against the lateral pelvic wall and psoas major by deep, unpadded lateral blades.

image.brief: Assembled Balfour self-retaining retractor with lateral wire blades, central bladder blade, and ratcheted frame on white sheet.

items.summary: A dual-ended retractor featuring two sharp stabilizing prongs on one side and a broad flat retractor blade on the other.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Solid steel retractor featuring two divergent pronged hooks at one terminal and a smooth, broad curved blade at the other.
Self-retaining frames bearing Czerny pattern blades are also utilised for abdominal wall retraction.
Pronged end provides solid purchase into fascial edges without slipping.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Retracting the superior and inferior aponeurotic margins during closure of midline laparotomy wounds.
Aids in exposure and placing the initial stabilizing mass-closure sutures across linea alba and rectus sheath.
Provides broad abdominal wall exposure during general pelvic and gynaecological operations.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: The pronged hooks must be placed strictly on dense fibrous sheath and never against delicate viscera.
Smooth opposite blade can be used interchangeably for non-penetrating abdominal wall retraction.

viva.q: What is the primary indication for using the pronged end of a Czerny retractor?
viva.a: Retracting the superior and inferior fascial margins of a midline laparotomy incision during mass closure of the abdominal wall.

viva.q: Why must the two prongs of the Czerny retractor not be applied against bowel?
viva.a: The sharp prongs easily pierce and tear intestinal serosa and muscularis, provoking perforation or visceral bleeding.

image.brief: Double-ended Czerny retractor showing two distinct terminal prongs at one end and flat curved blade at the other on neutral field.

items.summary: Flexible non-retaining red rubber and self-retaining winged Malecot catheters used for temporary urinary drainage and surgical tourniquets.

blocks.title: How to recognise them
bullets: Red rubber catheter: straight, flexible red latex tube with a blunt tip, a single side eyelet, and a tapered funnel connector.
Available in surgical sizes including 12, 14, 16, and 18 French gauge.
Malecot catheter: rubber catheter featuring two or four expandable slotted wings near the tip that hold position in a cavity.

groups.label: Red rubber catheter
bullets: Intermittent bladder catheterisation and collecting sterile urine specimens for culture and sensitivity.
Used as an elastic tourniquet around the uterine isthmus to compress uterine vessels and reduce blood loss in myomectomy.
Serving as a venous tourniquet for venepuncture, or providing nasal oxygen delivery in neonatal resuscitation.

groups.label: Malecot catheter
bullets: Temporary percutaneous urinary drainage following nephrostomy or suprapubic cystostomy.
Temporary feeding gastrostomy tube or draining pus, blood, and effusions from surgical cavities.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Red rubber catheter is non-self-retaining; Foley catheter is preferred for continuous drainage.
Malecot wings are collapsed using a rigid metal introducer during insertion and pop open upon stylet removal.

viva.q: How is a red rubber catheter utilized as a tourniquet during myomectomy?
viva.a: It is stretched tightly around the lower uterine segment at the internal os and clamped, temporarily occluding uterine vessels.

viva.q: How does a Malecot catheter maintain its position without an inflatable balloon?
viva.a: It features two or four preformed collapsible rubber wings near the tip that expand outward inside the drainage cavity.

items.summary: A flexible latex or silicone double-lumen indwelling catheter featuring an inflatable distal retention balloon for bladder drainage.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Flexible, sterile tube crafted from natural latex or silicone with a blunt rounded tip and lateral drainage eyelets.
Double-lumen design: primary larger port drains urine; secondary side arm with colour-coded valve connects to retention balloon.
The distal inflatable balloon typically holds 5 to 10 mL of sterile water to retain the catheter within the bladder neck.

groups.label: Gynaecological uses
bullets: Bladder decompression before and after abdominal hysterectomy, laparotomy, and pelvic floor repairs.
Management of acute or chronic urinary retention, and urinary drainage following vesicovaginal fistula (VVF) repair.
Diagnostic testing: instilling contrast in hysterosalpingography or saline infusion sonography (SIS).

groups.label: Obstetric uses
bullets: Bladder catheterisation prior to caesarean section, instrumental delivery, and management of obstructed labour.
Accurate hourly urine output monitoring in severe pre-eclampsia, eclampsia, and major obstetric haemorrhage.
Mechanical cervical ripening and induction of labour by extra-amniotic balloon inflation at the internal os.
Emergency intrauterine balloon tamponade (condom-Foley assembly) to control atonic postpartum haemorrhage (PPH).

blocks.title: Complications and cautions
bullets: Catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) with prolonged catheter dwell time.
Loss of detrusor bladder tone following extended continuous drainage, requiring bladder retraining.
Balloon must strictly be inflated with sterile water, never normal saline (crystallises valve) or air (floats away).

viva.q: Why should the Foley catheter balloon be inflated with sterile water rather than normal saline?
viva.a: Saline crystals can precipitate inside the inflation lumen, clogging the channel and preventing deflation during removal.

viva.q: How can a Foley catheter be adapted for emergency management of postpartum haemorrhage?
viva.a: A sterile condom is tied over the catheter tip and infused with saline inside the uterine cavity as an emergency tamponade balloon.

viva.q: How does a Foley catheter promote cervical ripening for induction of labour?
viva.a: The balloon is passed beyond the internal os and inflated, exerting direct mechanical pressure and stimulating endogenous prostaglandin release.

image.brief: Two-way latex Foley catheter displaying inflated distal retention balloon, drainage port, and colour-coded inflation valve on white drape.

items.summary: A short, rigid stainless steel tubular catheter with a blunt rounded tip and lateral drainage holes designed for female bladder evacuation.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Rigid, hollow stainless steel instrument measuring approximately 15 cm in length to accommodate the short female urethra.
Features a smooth, blunt rounded tip with two small opposing lateral drainage eyelets and a proximal expanded drainage funnel.
May be completely straight or possess a slight S-shaped or gentle anterior terminal curve.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Rapid decompression of the female urinary bladder before minor gynaecological interventions (D&C, fractional curettage).
Draining the bladder in acute or chronic urinary retention when flexible catheters encounter resistance.
Sounding and outlining the bladder base before making an inverted-T anterior vaginal wall incision in vaginal hysterectomy.

blocks.title: Points to remember

viva.q: What are the two components of a laparoscopic port assembly and their respective roles?

viva.q: What life-threatening complication can occur during initial blind umbilical trocar insertion?

viva.q: How does the spring-loaded blunt stylet in a Veress needle protect internal organs?

items.summary: A rigid optical telescope containing Hopkins rod lenses and optical fibre bundles used to illuminate and visualise the peritoneal cavity.

45-degree and 70-degree angled scopes: utilised for specialized deep retroperitoneal dissection and visualisation behind dense adhesions.

blocks.title: Comparison of 0-degree and angled scopes
bullets: 0-degree scope: easier to operate with direct centred field, but cannot visualise hidden lateral recesses and corners.
Angled scope: superior for visualising hidden recesses without blocking instrument paths, but requires camera coordination to avoid disorientation.

viva.q: What is the primary advantage of a thirty-degree laparoscope over a zero-degree scope?
viva.a: Rotating the thirty-degree scope allows panoramic inspection behind structures and into pelvic recesses like the pouch of Douglas without moving the port.

viva.q: What internal optical system is utilized in modern rigid laparoscopes?
viva.a: The Hopkins rod-lens system, which uses solid quartz glass rods with miniature air spaces to provide bright, high-resolution optical images.

image.brief: Ten-millimetre thirty-degree rigid laparoscopic telescope on black velvet showing ocular lens, light cable post, and angled distal tip.

items.summary: A long, insulated rigid laparoscopic shaft terminating in a smooth rounded probe tip used for atraumatic tissue plane separation.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Insulated 5 mm rigid instrument with a textured proximal handle and an elongated shaft.
Working tip consists of a smooth, polished, non-cutting rounded bulb or blunt spatula.
Features no sharp cutting edges or pinching teeth.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Atraumatic blunt separation of tissue planes, such as stripping an ovarian endometrioma or dermoid cyst capsule from healthy ovarian cortex.
Palpating pelvic viscera, mobilizing loose bowel loops, and identifying retroperitoneal anatomical landmarks without piercing serosa.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Minimises accidental vascular laceration and visceral perforation during plane dissection.
Can be equipped with monopolar electrocautery capability in select designs.

viva.q: What is the primary role of a laparoscopic blunt dissector during ovarian cystectomy?
viva.a: Peeling and separating the fibrous cyst wall capsule away from normal ovarian cortex without puncturing the cyst or tearing vessels.

viva.q: Why is blunt dissection favoured over sharp dissection when developing loose pelvic planes?
viva.a: It follows natural avascular anatomical clefts, preventing bleeding and protecting retroperitoneal nerves and vessels.

items.summary: A ratcheted or non-ratcheted 5 mm laparoscopic instrument with curved, fine tapering serrated jaws used for delicate dissection.

blocks.title: Uses

Mobilising and pushing the uterovesical peritoneal fold and bladder flap downward during laparoscopic hysterectomy.
Surgically dissecting around the uterine artery and skeletonizing vascular pedicles prior to sealing.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: The gently curved tip allows the surgeon to spread tissue planes outward (push-and-spread blunt dissection).
Fine tapered jaws enable selective grasping and isolation of small bleeding vessels.

viva.q: How is the curved Maryland dissector used to develop the bladder flap in laparoscopic hysterectomy?
viva.a: It gently spreads and pushes the loose connective tissue of the uterovesical fold, mobilizing the bladder down away from the cervix.

viva.q: What motion is utilized when performing blunt dissection with Maryland forceps?
viva.a: The closed jaws are introduced into the tissue plane and then opened gently, separating planes along natural anatomical lines.

items.summary: A 5 mm laparoscopic cutting instrument with curved, micro-serrated blades and monopolar cautery connection for sharp dissection.

Handle features a high-frequency monopolar electrocautery post.

blocks.title: Uses

Incising the round ligament, utero-ovarian ligament, and broad ligament sheets during laparoscopic hysterectomy.
Simultaneous sharp transection and electrosurgical coagulation of small capillary bleeders.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Curved design ensures tip visibility during cuts and prevents obscuring the transection zone.
Monopolar current must be activated only when blades are in direct vision, avoiding collateral thermal damage to bowel or ureter.

viva.q: What is the primary danger when using monopolar cautery with laparoscopic scissors near the pelvic sidewall?
viva.a: Unintended thermal conduction or stray current sparking to the ureter or iliac vessels, resulting in delayed thermal necrosis.

viva.q: Why are the blades of laparoscopic dissecting scissors curved?
viva.a: The curve allows the surgeon to visualize the exact tips of the blades during cutting, preventing inadvertent injury to underlying structures.

items.summary: A heavy 5 mm or 10 mm laparoscopic grasper with sharp interlocking teeth engineered to hold tough fibroids and tissue for extraction.

Securing large tissue specimens during extraction through expanded port sites.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Highly traumatic instrument: never apply to bowel, urinary bladder, fallopian tubes, or tissues intended for preservation.
The interlocking teeth cause localized puncture and necrosis of grasped tissue.

viva.q: When is a laparoscopic toothed claw grasper indicated?
viva.a: When strong mechanical traction is required on tough tissues destined for excision, such as a uterine fibroid or thick ovarian cyst wall.

viva.q: Why is toothed grasper strictly contraindicated on bowel during laparoscopy?
viva.a: The sharp interlocking teeth inflict full-thickness puncture lacerations on thin visceral walls, causing bowel perforation and peritonitis.

Manufactured without sharp teeth or cutting edges to protect delicate organs.

Handling the urinary bladder flap and holding pelvic peritoneum without inducing serosal hematoma.

viva.q: What design characteristics make a laparoscopic grasper atraumatic?
viva.a: Blunt rounded tips, broad fenestrated jaws, and undulating wave serrations that distribute tension without sharp teeth or cutting edges.

viva.q: Which organs during gynaecological laparoscopy require the use of an atraumatic grasper?
viva.a: The fallopian tubes, small and large intestine, and the urinary bladder, where puncture or crush trauma must be strictly avoided.

items.summary: A transvaginally placed instrument used to antevert, retrovert, elevate, and lateralise the uterus during pelvic laparoscopy.

Equipped with an external ergonomic handle and locking articulation lever for directional manipulation.

viva.q: What is the primary surgical purpose of a uterine manipulator in laparoscopic hysterectomy?
viva.a: It provides multidirectional manipulation to expose pelvic anatomy and delineates the vaginal fornices for safe colpotomy.

viva.q: How does the uterine manipulator protect the ureters during laparoscopic hysterectomy?
viva.a: By pushing the cervix upward and forward, it increases the distance between the uterine artery ligation site and the ureter.

items.summary: A dual-channel laparoscopic probe system with trumpet valves used to deliver pressurized fluid irrigation and evacuate blood and smoke.

Evacuating blood clots, cystic fluid, and purulent exudate in ruptured ectopic pregnancy and pelvic inflammatory disease.
Clearing electrosurgical aerosol smoke and steam to maintain crisp optical visualization.
Performing gentle blunt hydrodissection to separate loose retroperitoneal tissue planes.

viva.a: It rapidly aspirates haemoperitoneum and clots, allowing lavaging of the pelvis to identify and control the tubal bleeding site.

viva.q: What complication occurs if the suction trumpet button is depressed continuously for too long?
viva.a: Rapid loss of the carbon dioxide pneumoperitoneum, causing loss of laparoscopic visualization and abdominal wall collapse.

viva.q: What are the recommended energy settings and puncture parameters for laparoscopic ovarian drilling?
viva.a: Four to five punctures per ovary using forty watts of power, each crater measuring under 4 mm in diameter and approximately 4 mm deep.

viva.q: What is the physiological objective of laparoscopic ovarian drilling in PCOS?
viva.a: It destroys androgen-producing thecal stroma, decreasing intraovarian androgens and LH levels to trigger spontaneous ovulation.

items.summary: A 5 mm laparoscopic grasping forceps featuring multiple fine interlocking teeth designed to hold tough fascial margins.

Bowed jaw design encloses an open clearance space when the tips are locked.

blocks.title: Uses

Holding excised benign fibroids or cystic walls during operative extraction.
Providing firm, slip-resistant grip on fibrous structures intended for excision.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Semi-traumatic design: provides firmer traction than atraumatic graspers but causes more crush injury.
Never apply to bowel, urinary bladder, or fallopian tubes intended for functional preservation.

viva.q: When is a laparoscopic Allis forceps indicated during pelvic surgery?
viva.a: For grasping tough fibrous structures like the vaginal cuff during colpotomy or dense fascial and peritoneal edges.

viva.q: Why is the laparoscopic Allis forceps avoided on healthy bowel loops?
viva.a: Its multiple fine interlocking teeth exert high focal pressure that can lacerate the intestinal seromuscular wall.

image.brief: Five-millimetre laparoscopic Allis forceps showing insulated black shaft, ratchet handle, and open jaws with interlocking comb teeth.

items.summary: An atraumatic 5 mm or 10 mm laparoscopic forceps with smooth, triangular fenestrated loops designed to cradle tubular structures.

Jaws expand into smooth, paddle-shaped triangular fenestrated loops without teeth or sharp edges.
Meeting rims cradle tissues gently without increasing intraluminal pressure.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Grasping and manipulating fallopian tubes during laparoscopic salpingectomy, tubectomy, and tubal reanastomosis.
Holding delicate loops of small or large bowel, ureters, and appendix without inflicting serosal trauma.
Elevating pelvic peritoneal folds during diagnostic laparoscopy.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Non-perforating and completely atraumatic to tubular visceral lumens.
The fenestrated loop allows visualization of underlying tissue while providing gentle grasping traction.

viva.q: Why is the laparoscopic Babcock forceps preferred for handling the fallopian tube?
viva.a: Its broad, smooth fenestrated jaws distribute holding tension gently, preventing crush injury and preserving tubal vascularity.

viva.q: What other pelvic organs can be safely manipulated with a laparoscopic Babcock forceps?
viva.a: Loops of small and large bowel, the vermiform appendix, and the ureter during retroperitoneal dissection.

Closing the vaginal vault following total laparoscopic hysterectomy (TLH).
Securing synthetic mesh to the sacral promontory in laparoscopic sacrocolpopexy.
Facilitating intracorporeal knot tying and knot pushing in laparoscopic surgery.

bullets: The short jaw length maximizes mechanical leverage and holding force on surgical needles.
Requires practice to master the needle transfer and driving angle through fixed laparoscopic port vectors.

viva.q: What design feature prevents the suture needle from rotating within a laparoscopic needle holder?
viva.a: Tungsten carbide inserts with diamond-cut cross-hatched serrations on the short, rigid jaws.

viva.q: What are the common clinical applications of laparoscopic suturing in gynaecology?
viva.a: Multilayer repair of the myometrium after myomectomy, closing the vaginal vault after TLH, and anchoring sacrocolpopexy mesh.

items.summary: A 5 mm or 10 mm rigid laparoscopic probe ending in a sharp corkscrew tip used to provide solid traction on uterine fibroids.

Stabilising large leiomyomas during electromechanical morcellation.

viva.q: How is the laparoscopic myoma screw deployed during myomectomy?
viva.a: It is introduced through a secondary trocar and rotated clockwise directly into the fibroid core to provide mechanical traction.

viva.q: Why is the myoma screw preferred over standard graspers for large intramural fibroids?
viva.a: Rubbery fibroids slip easily from graspers; the corkscrew anchors deeply into the dense core to exert substantial traction.

items.summary: An intelligent bipolar electrosurgical vessel sealing device delivering high current and low voltage to permanently seal vessels up to 7 mm.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Computerized feedback automatically adjusts voltage and terminates energy delivery when sealing is complete, reducing surgeon variability.

Features superior burst pressure performance compared to conventional bipolar systems.

viva.q: What vessel diameter can the LigaSure system reliably seal?

viva.q: How does the electrical profile of LigaSure differ from conventional electrosurgery?
viva.a: LigaSure delivers high current and low voltage, in contrast to conventional electrosurgery which relies on low current and high voltage.

viva.q: What is the biological mechanism of vessel sealing achieved by LigaSure?
viva.a: It denatures collagen and elastin in the vessel wall under pressure, which then cross-link during cooling into a permanent seal.

items.summary: An ultrasonic surgical shears vibrating at 55,000 Hz that converts acoustic mechanical energy into low-temperature cutting and coagulation.

Vessel sealing efficacy depends on power setting, blade pressure, and tissue tension applied by the surgeon.
Produces minimal lateral thermal spread and minimal smoke compared to high-voltage electrosurgical devices.

viva.q: What is the operational frequency of the Harmonic scalpel?
viva.a: It vibrates longitudinally at fifty-five thousand cycles per second (55 kHz), driven by a piezoelectric acoustic transducer.

viva.q: What temperature range does the Harmonic scalpel generate in tissue?
viva.a: It operates at fifty to one hundred degrees Celsius, significantly lower than the temperatures created by conventional electrosurgery.

image.brief: Harmonic scalpel laparoscopic shears showing ergonomic handgrip, dual power buttons, and active vibrating blade with clamp pad.

items.summary: An electromechanical surgical device with a high-speed rotating hollow circular blade used to fragment and extract large tissues.

Equipped with a protective outer safety shield and variable-speed foot pedal control.

bullets: Cores large uterine masses and fibroids into long cylindrical strips of tissue during myomectomy and hysterectomy.
Allows large solid specimens to be extracted through standard minimally invasive laparoscopic abdominal ports.
Reduces incision size, post-operative wound infection, pain, and hospital recovery times.

viva.q: What is the primary oncological hazard of uncontained power morcellation?
viva.a: Dissemination of an occult uterine leiomyosarcoma throughout the peritoneal cavity, which significantly worsens stage and prognosis.

viva.q: How does enclosed or in-bag morcellation improve patient safety?
viva.a: It confines all fragmented tissue strips and cellular debris within an impervious retrieval bag, preventing peritoneal seeding.

items.summary: A sterile deployable polymer containment bag with an elastic memory-metal opening ring used to extract surgical specimens cleanly.

viva.a: To prevent sebaceous fluid and hair from spilling into the peritoneal cavity, which provokes severe chemical peritonitis and dense adhesions.

viva.q: How is a large specimen removed through a smaller trocar incision using a retrieval bag?

items.summary: A specialized laparoscopic dual-cylinder applicator used to draw in a loop of fallopian tube and apply a silastic constricting ring.

blocks.title: Operative technique and points to remember
bullets: The tongs grasp the ampullary-isthmic junction of the fallopian tube and gently draw an 8 to 10 mm knuckle into the inner cylinder.
Advancing the outer cylinder pushes the stretched silastic band off the barrel, snapping it securely around the base of the tubal loop.
The ring causes localized avascular necrosis and fibrous occlusion of the lumen; mesosalpingeal tears must be avoided.

viva.q: How does the Falope ring achieve permanent female tubal occlusion?
viva.a: The elastic silastic ring constricts a knuckle of the fallopian tube, inducing localized ischaemic necrosis and luminal fibrosis.

viva.q: What complication can arise if excessive traction is applied to the fallopian tube during band application?
viva.a: Tearing of the vascular mesosalpinx, causing brisk pelvic haemorrhage and haematoma formation requiring laparoscopic coagulation.

items.summary: An integrated endoscopic system consisting of a rigid telescope, double sheath, distension media, camera, and light source for uterine cavity inspection.

blocks.title: System components
bullets: Endoscopic optical telescope: rigid telescope measuring 2 to 4 mm in diameter with eyepiece and objective lenses.
Outer sheath assembly: 3 to 5 mm outer sheath with stopcock channels for continuous inflow and outflow of distension media.
Fibreoptic light cable and high-intensity illumination source (halogen or xenon).
Digital video camera head, processing console, and high-definition colour monitor.
Uterine distension media delivery system and electrosurgical or mechanical operative instruments.

blocks.title: Ancillary instruments and uses
bullets: Operating channels allow insertion of miniaturized hysteroscopic instruments through a 1 mm clearance space.
Hysteroscopic scissors: incising uterine septa, fine intrauterine synechiae, or clipping polyps.
Cullen knife and electrosurgical electrodes: cutting, resecting, and coagulating submucosal fibroids and septa.
Biopsy and grasping forceps: taking targeted endometrial biopsies and extracting tissue fragments under direct vision.
Intrauterine morcellator: cutting and evacuating large fibroids and polyps mechanically.

blocks.title: Distension media principles
bullets: Liquid distension media: normal saline is standard for bipolar devices; non-conductive fluids (glycine) for monopolar electrosurgery.
Strict fluid deficit tracking is mandatory to avoid fluid overload, pulmonary oedema, and dilutional hyponatraemia.

viva.q: What are the core hardware components of a complete hysteroscopy system?
viva.a: Rigid telescope, operating and continuous-flow sheaths, light source and cable, digital camera system, and distension media pump.

viva.q: Why is fluid deficit tracking critical during operative hysteroscopy?
viva.a: Excessive systemic absorption of distension media through opened venous sinuses can cause life-threatening fluid overload and hyponatraemia.

image.brief: Modular hysteroscopy assembly displaying telescope inside operating sheath with dual stopcocks, light cable, and camera coupling.

items.summary: A 30-degree fore-oblique optical telescope designed to provide panoramic inspection of the uterine cavity and tubal ostia.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Slender rigid optical telescope with a distal prism angled at 30 degrees to the long optical axis.
Fits inside a calibrated continuous-flow outer sheath with dedicated channels for fluid inflow and outflow.
Provides a continuous stream of distension fluid to keep the optical view washed and free of blood.

blocks.title: Three-component assembly
bullets: Outer sheath: directs continuous flow of distension media into and out of the uterine cavity.
Telescope: 30-degree optical rod lens that delivers panoramic illumination and visualization.
Operating instrument: passes through the dedicated working channel alongside the telescope.

blocks.title: Clinical advantages
bullets: Rotating the light post 360 degrees allows comprehensive panoramic survey of the uterine fundus, walls, and tubal ostia.
Enables inspection into the lateral cornua without requiring severe angulation of the patient cervix.

viva.q: What is the primary advantage of a 30-degree hysteroscope over a straight 0-degree scope?
viva.a: Rotating the 30-degree telescope provides panoramic visualization of the tubal ostia and cornua without excessive cervical manipulation.

viva.q: What is the function of the continuous-flow double sheath on the 30-degree hysteroscope?
viva.a: It simultaneously introduces fresh distension fluid and evacuates blood, mucus, and bubbles to maintain continuous visual clarity.

image.brief: Thirty-degree angled hysteroscope nestled inside its metallic double sheath with continuous flow stopcocks on blue clinical backdrop.

items.summary: A smooth blunt-nosed metal introducer fitted inside the outer resectoscope sheath to facilitate atraumatic cervical entry.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Solid stainless steel shaft with a proximal locking hub and a smooth, bullet-shaped rounded blunt tip.
When locked into the resectoscope outer sheath, its blunt rounded nose protrudes just beyond the sharp distal rim.
Available as a standard rigid blunt obturator or a visual obturator with a channel for a telescope.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Introduced inside the large-bore outer resectoscope sheath during insertion through the dilated cervical canal.
Prevents the sharp, bevelled leading edge of the resectoscope sheath from gouging, tearing, or perforating the cervix.
Withdrawn once the sheath enters the endometrial cavity, making way for the working element and optical telescope.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: The cervix must be dilated with Hegar dilators to match the outer French gauge of the sheath before introducing the obturator.
Advanced gently along the known axis of uterine flexion to avoid cervical false passage.

viva.q: What is the primary purpose of using an obturator with a hysteroscopic resectoscope sheath?
viva.a: It blunts the sharp distal rim of the wide resectoscope sheath, preventing cervical laceration and false tracking during insertion.

viva.q: What step immediately follows introduction of the resectoscope sheath into the uterine cavity?
viva.a: The obturator is unlocked and removed, and the telescope and working resectoscope element are locked into the sheath.

image.brief: Smooth stainless steel resectoscope obturator shown beside the hollow outer sheath with continuous flow ports on white tray.

items.summary: A specialized electrosurgical endoscopic instrument assembly used to perform intrauterine resection of fibroids, polyps, and endometrium.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Modular surgical assembly consisting of an inner and outer continuous-flow sheath, an optical telescope, and a working handle.
Working element features a spring-loaded finger slider (passive or active mechanism) to advance and retract electrosurgical electrodes.
Accepts interchangeable specialized electrode tips including loop, rollerball, roller barrel, and Collins knife.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Transcervical resection of the endometrium (TCRE) for abnormal uterine bleeding resistant to medical management.
Hysteroscopic resection of submucosal leiomyomas (FIGO Type 0, 1, and 2 fibroids) and large endometrial polyps.
Hysteroscopic metroplasty for congenital uterine septa and division of dense Asherman synechiae.

blocks.title: Monopolar versus bipolar systems
bullets: Monopolar resectoscopes require non-electrolyte distension fluid (such as 1.5% glycine) and carry risks of dilutional hyponatraemia.
Bipolar resectoscopes operate safely in physiological normal saline, significantly reducing the risks of hyponatraemic encephalopathy.

viva.q: What distension fluid is used with a bipolar hysteroscopic resectoscope and why?
viva.a: Physiological 0.9% normal saline, which eliminates the dangerous risk of acute dilutional hyponatraemia seen with non-electrolyte fluids.

viva.q: What are the primary clinical indications for hysteroscopic resectoscopy in gynaecology?
viva.a: Endometrial ablation for abnormal bleeding, resection of submucosal fibroids and polyps, and division of uterine septa.

image.brief: Complete hysteroscopic resectoscope assembly with spring working handle, double sheath, telescope, and electrode mounted on clean field.

items.summary: A specialized wire loop electrode mounted on a resectoscope working element used to shave and resect intracavitary lesions.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Long insulated dual-arm carrier that locks into the resectoscope working element.
Tip consists of a semicircular or angled tungsten wire loop positioned perpendicular to the optical lens axis.
Available in straight and angled cutting orientations in varying widths.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Resecting and slicing submucosal fibroids in chips from the fundus and uterine walls.
Excision of broad-based and pedunculated endometrial polyps under direct vision.
Performing systematic endometrial resection strips during transcervical resection of the endometrium (TCRE).

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Energy must only be activated while drawing the loop backwards towards the resectoscope sheath under direct visual control.
Never push an energized loop forward into the myometrium, which carries high risk of uterine perforation and bowel injury.

viva.q: What direction of cutting stroke is mandatory when using a hysteroscopic loop electrode?
viva.a: Cutting must always be performed on the backward pull toward the resectoscope sheath under direct visualization, never pushing forward.

viva.q: What dangerous complication can occur if a loop electrode is energized while pushing forward against the fundus?
viva.a: Uterine wall perforation with high risk of electrical and thermal burn injury to underlying bowel loops or pelvic vessels.

image.brief: Fine tungsten wire loop resectoscope electrode showing long insulated carrier shafts and semicircular cutting loop at the tip.

items.summary: A straight or right-angled fine wire needle electrode used for precise focal incision of uterine septa, synechiae, and dense fibroids.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Insulated electrode stem terminating in a short, straight or right-angled fine tungsten cutting needle or knife wire.
Engineered for highly localized electrosurgical cutting rather than tissue shaving.
Connects to the resectoscope working element in place of a cutting loop.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Hysteroscopic metroplasty: dividing congenital uterine septa until a symmetrical triangular uterine cavity is established.
Lysis of dense intrauterine synechiae and fibrotic bands in severe Asherman syndrome.
Incising the capsule of deep intramural fibroids to allow them to prolapse into the endometrial cavity.
Precise division of cervical canal synechiae and strictures.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Provides pinpoint cutting with minimal collateral thermal damage to the surrounding healthy endometrium.
Septal incision is continued until bleeding points indicate transition to vascular myometrium and both ostia align symmetrically.

viva.q: What is the primary role of the Collins knife in hysteroscopic reproductive surgery?
viva.a: Accurate division and resection of a congenital uterine septum (metroplasty) and lysis of dense intrauterine synechiae.

viva.q: What anatomical sign indicates that septal division with a Collins knife is complete?
viva.a: Appearance of healthy vascular myometrium with slight pink capillary bleeding and uniform alignment of both tubal ostia.

image.brief: Collins knife hysteroscopic electrode showing insulated long stem and sharp right-angled tungsten cutting needle tip on neutral background.

items.summary: A spherical revolving metallic electrode mounted on a resectoscope carrier used for electrosurgical endometrial ablation.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Insulated dual-wire resectoscope electrode terminating in a revolving solid metallic sphere (typically 2 mm to 4 mm in diameter).
Alternative barrel design features a rotating cylindrical metallic roller.
Revolves smoothly across the mucosal surface without catching or cutting into tissue.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Endometrial ablation for treatment of heavy menstrual bleeding in women who have completed childbearing.
Coagulating bleeding vessels across the endometrial cavity following loop resection of fibroids or polyps.
Ablating endometrium over difficult cornual recesses where cutting loops pose high perforation risks.

blocks.title: Mechanism and points to remember
bullets: Delivers high-frequency coagulation current as it rolls over the endometrium, producing thermal coagulation to a depth of 2 to 3 mm.
Destroys the basalis layer of the endometrium to prevent post-operative mucosal regeneration.
Pre-treatment with GnRH agonists or progestins thins the endometrium prior to rollerball ablation to enhance success.

viva.q: What depth of thermal destruction is achieved by a hysteroscopic rollerball electrode?
viva.a: It produces thermal coagulation necrosis to a depth of two to three millimetres, destroying the regenerative basal layer.

viva.q: Why is medical pre-treatment often administered before rollerball endometrial ablation?
viva.a: Agents like GnRH agonists or progestins thin the endometrium, maximizing ablation depth and improving amenorrhoea rates.

image.brief: Hysteroscopic rollerball electrode displaying insulated stem and polished metallic revolving spherical ball tip on clean drape.

title.en: Endoscopic camera and light source tower

items.summary: An integrated video and illumination stack console comprising a medical-grade HD monitor, cold light source, and camera control unit.

blocks.title: System components
bullets: Medical-grade high-definition (HD or 4K) colour video monitor positioned at eye level for the surgical team.
High-intensity cold light source generator utilizing xenon, LED, or halogen lamps with automated brightness adjustment.
Digital camera control unit (CCU) connected to a sterilizable high-definition camera head.
Flexible fibreoptic or fluid-filled light cable transmitting cold light from the console to the telescope.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Illuminating, capturing, transmitting, and displaying magnified real-time video during laparoscopy and hysteroscopy.
Enabling the entire surgical team, anaesthetist, and nurses to visualize the operative field synchronously.
Capturing digital still photographs and video recordings for patient documentation and educational review.

blocks.title: Operational precautions
bullets: White balance calibration must be performed against a clean white surgical swab prior to inserting the scope.
Light cables must not be bent sharply, dropped, or coiled tightly, to prevent fracturing fragile internal glass fibres.
The high-intensity light cable tip becomes intensely hot and must never rest directly on patient skin or paper drapes.

viva.q: Why must white balancing be performed before commencing an endoscopic procedure?
viva.a: To calibrate the camera sensor to the specific light spectrum, ensuring accurate intraoperative tissue colour reproduction.

viva.q: What physical hazard is associated with the disconnected tip of a fibreoptic light cable?
viva.a: High thermal output from the tip can cause full-thickness patient skin burns or ignite combustible surgical drapes.
